title: ARE TONGUES AND PROPHECY STILL REAL TODAY—OR HAVE WE BEEN MISTAKING EMOTION FOR THE HOLY SPIRIT?
paragraphs: ARE TONGUES AND PROPHECY STILL REAL TODAY—OR HAVE WE BEEN MISTAKING EMOTION FOR THE HOLY SPIRIT?

Some Christians say the gifts of the Spirit have ceased. Others say every believer should speak in tongues and prophesy. But what if the greatest danger isn't being on the wrong side of the debate—it's being so consumed by spiritual power that we forget the Savior who gives it?
There is a kind of silence that can break a Christian's heart.
Not the silence of an empty church.
Not the silence after the final worship song.
But the silence of someone who has begged God for years to experience what everyone else seems to have experienced.
You watched people fall to their knees. You heard voices rise in languages you couldn't understand. You listened as someone declared, "The Lord told me..."
And somewhere beneath the music, the tears, and the trembling hands, you whispered something you were almost ashamed to admit.
"Jesus... why not me?"
Maybe you have spent years wondering whether something is missing from your relationship with God.
Maybe someone told you that unless you speak in tongues, you haven't truly received the Holy Spirit.
Maybe you grew up in a church where prophecy was treated as ordinary, until someone supposedly speaking for God wounded you with words that never came true.
Or maybe you come from the opposite side.

You were taught that tongues and prophecy disappeared when the apostles died. Every modern claim made you suspicious. Every emotional worship service seemed dangerous. And every testimony of the supernatural sounded like something that needed to be exposed.
Then one day, someone you trusted told you about an experience you couldn't easily dismiss.
And suddenly the question became personal.
Are tongues and prophecy still active today?
Can the Holy Spirit still distribute these gifts?
Or are Christians chasing experiences that God never promised to continue?
And perhaps the question that should trouble us most...
If the Holy Spirit truly is at work, would we recognize Him—or would we be too busy defending our traditions to listen to Scripture?
Before we answer, we need to go somewhere more reliable than testimonies, denominations, viral videos, or the loudest preacher in the room.
We need to return to the Word of God.
Because the Holy Spirit never needs us to abandon the Scriptures in order to experience His presence.
And Jesus never asked His Church to choose between truth and the Spirit who inspired it.
When the apostle Paul wrote to the believers in Corinth, he was addressing a church overflowing with spiritual activity—and deeply troubled by spiritual immaturity.
Think about that.
They were not lacking religious experiences.
They were lacking love, order, humility, and discernment.
Paul acknowledged that they were not lacking in any spiritual gift as they waited for the revealing of Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 1:7).
Yet the same church was divided, proud, morally compromised, and confused about worship.
They had gifts.
But gifts did not automatically mean maturity.
They had knowledge.
But knowledge had become a reason for boasting.
They had extraordinary spiritual experiences.
But ordinary Christian love was being neglected.
Does that sound painfully familiar?
A person can speak beautifully about the supernatural and still speak cruelly to their family.
Someone can claim to prophesy over nations and still refuse to repent of private sin.
A preacher can fill a room with excitement and still fail to care for the wounded people sitting in the back row.
And a Christian can be so determined to expose false spiritual experiences that they forget to demonstrate the gentleness of Christ.
The Corinthian church reminds us of a truth that should humble every side of this conversation.
The presence of a spiritual gift is not proof of spiritual maturity. And the absence of a particular gift is not proof of spiritual inferiority.
Paul makes that unmistakably clear in 1 Corinthians 12.
He writes:
—1 Corinthians 12:4, King James Version
The Greek word translated "gifts" is χαρισμάτων (charismatōn), the plural of χάρισμα (charisma).
It comes from the same word family as χάρις (charis), meaning grace or favor.
This matters.
Because spiritual gifts are not medals awarded to the most impressive Christians.
They are gracious gifts distributed by God.
You cannot earn them through spiritual performance.
You cannot manufacture them through emotional intensity.
And you cannot turn them into a ranking system without contradicting the very grace from which they come.
Paul continues:
"But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal."
—1 Corinthians 12:7, KJV
The phrase "to profit withal" means for the common good.
The Greek expression is πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον (pros to sympheron).
The point is not personal celebrity.
Not religious superiority.
Not the ability to impress a congregation.
The Spirit's gifts are given for the benefit of Christ's body.
Then Paul names gifts including wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment of spirits, various kinds of tongues, and interpretation of tongues.
But notice what happens in verse 11.
Paul says the Spirit distributes these gifts "to every man severally as he will."
The Greek phrase καθὼς βούλεται (kathōs bouletai) means "as He wills."
Not as the preacher demands.
Not as the congregation expects.
Not as religious pressure dictates.
As the Holy Spirit wills.
And this immediately corrects one of the most painful teachings some Christians have encountered.
The Bible does not teach that every Christian must speak in tongues to prove that the Holy Spirit lives within them.
Paul asks in 1 Corinthians 12:30:
"Do all speak with tongues? do all interpret?"
The expected answer in the Greek construction is no.
Different members receive different gifts.
The body needs all its members.
And the believer who does not speak in tongues is not therefore a second-class Christian.
Romans 8:9 teaches that belonging to Christ and having the Spirit are inseparable.
Ephesians 1:13 describes believers as sealed with the promised Holy Spirit when they believed the Gospel.
Your salvation is not secured by producing a particular spiritual manifestation.
Your salvation rests in Jesus Christ.
His death.
His resurrection.
His grace received through faith.
And if someone has made you feel that Jesus is insufficient unless you can reproduce their experience, you need to hear this clearly.
Christ is not incomplete because your spiritual experience looks different from someone else's.
But does that mean tongues and prophecy have ceased?
To understand the question, we must return to the day the Church was born.
Jerusalem.
Pentecost.
A gathering of disciples waiting as Jesus commanded.
Then a sound like a mighty rushing wind.
Tongues resembling fire.
And people speaking in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.
Acts 2:4 says:
"And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance."
The Greek word translated "tongues" is γλώσσαις (glōssais), from γλῶσσα (glōssa), which can refer to the physical tongue or to a language.
And Acts 2 gives us a crucial detail.
The crowd heard the disciples speaking in their own languages.
Acts 2:8 uses διαλέκτῳ (dialektō), referring to a language or dialect.
People from different regions heard the mighty works of God proclaimed in words they could understand.
This was not a performance designed to glorify the disciples.
It was a sign that the Gospel of Jesus Christ was breaking through human boundaries.
The message that began in Jerusalem was destined for the nations.
And Peter explained what was happening by quoting the prophet Joel.
"And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy..."
—Acts 2:17, KJV
In Joel 2:28, the Hebrew expression for "I will pour out my Spirit" is:
אֶשְׁפּוֹךְ אֶת־רוּחִי
'eshpokh 'et-ruchi
The image is of God pouring out His Spirit.
Not a trickle reserved for an elite religious class.
Not a privilege determined by social status.
Peter announces that the promised age of the Spirit has arrived through the exalted Jesus Christ.
Sons and daughters.
Young and old.
Servants, men and women.
God's promise was reaching people the world might have overlooked.
But Peter did not conclude his sermon by telling everyone to pursue spectacular experiences.
He proclaimed Jesus.
Jesus crucified.
Jesus raised from the dead.
Jesus exalted at the right hand of God.
And when the people were pierced to the heart, they asked what they should do.
Peter called them to repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.
The supernatural event pointed to the crucified and risen Savior.
That is the pattern we must never lose.
The Holy Spirit does not compete with Jesus for attention. He glorifies Jesus.
Christ Himself taught this in John 16:14:
"He shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall shew it unto you."
So whenever someone claims to be operating in the power of the Holy Spirit, a question must be asked.
Where is Jesus in all of this?
Is Christ being exalted?
Is Scripture being honored?
Are sinners being called to repentance?
Are believers being strengthened in truth and love?
Or has the experience itself become the object of worship?
Because even a genuinely extraordinary experience becomes spiritually dangerous when it displaces the Lord it should honor.
Now we come to the passage that has divided sincere Christians for generations.
First Corinthians 13.
Paul writes:
—1 Corinthians 13:8, KJV
Some Christians read this and conclude that prophecy and tongues were temporary gifts intended for the apostolic age.
They argue that these gifts served a foundational purpose as the Church was established and the apostolic message was confirmed.
This position is commonly called cessationism.
Its defenders often appeal to passages such as Ephesians 2:20, which describes the Church as built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Jesus Christ as the chief cornerstone.
They also emphasize the unique authority of the apostles and the sufficiency of the completed Scriptures.
Their concern deserves to be heard seriously.
God's people must not be governed by new claims of revelation that rival the Bible.
No modern prophet possesses the authority to rewrite the Gospel.
No spiritual experience can overturn apostolic teaching.
No supposed message from heaven can correct the Word God has already given.
But other faithful Christians read the same passages and reach a different conclusion.
They believe the New Testament gifts may continue until Christ returns, while insisting that every claim must be tested by Scripture.
This position is commonly called continuationism.
They point out that 1 Corinthians 13:8 does not, by itself, tell us exactly when tongues and prophecy cease.
Paul continues:
"For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away."
—1 Corinthians 13:9–10, KJV
The Greek phrase translated "that which is perfect" is τὸ τέλειον (to teleion).
The word teleion can mean complete, mature, or brought to its intended end, depending on context.
Some interpret this completion as the arrival of the completed New Testament canon or the maturity of the apostolic Church.
Others argue that Paul's following words point beyond the present age.
He writes:
—1 Corinthians 13:12, KJV
The Greek phrase πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον (prosōpon pros prosōpon) means "face to face."

Continuationists argue that this language most naturally describes the fullness of knowledge and direct encounter associated with Christ's return, rather than merely the completion of the biblical canon.
That is a substantial contextual argument.
But we must also acknowledge something important.
Christians who affirm the authority of Scripture and the lordship of Jesus have genuinely disagreed about this passage.
The Bible does not explicitly state, "All miraculous gifts will end immediately upon the death of the last apostle."
Neither does it explicitly guarantee that every manifestation reported in every generation is authentic.
We must distinguish what Scripture clearly teaches from conclusions that require interpretation.
And we must be careful not to confuse confidence with infallibility.
There is a difference between defending biblical truth and pretending that our interpretation of every difficult passage is beyond examination.
Consider another instruction Paul gives.
"Wherefore, brethren, covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues."
—1 Corinthians 14:39, KJV
That is a real apostolic command to the Corinthian church.
Continuationists reasonably ask why Christians today should assume it no longer applies without compelling biblical evidence.
Cessationists respond that instructions concerning particular gifts may belong to the period in which those gifts were operative.
This is precisely where the debate lies.
Not between people who love the Bible and people who hate it.
Not automatically between Spirit-filled believers and spiritually dead believers.
But between different understandings of how the New Testament describes the purpose and duration of certain gifts.
We should be willing to examine those arguments without caricaturing our brothers and sisters.
Yet whatever position we hold, we cannot escape the instructions Paul gives concerning spiritual activity.
"Let all things be done unto edifying."
—1 Corinthians 14:26, KJV
"Let all things be done decently and in order."
—1 Corinthians 14:40, KJV
These are not optional decorations.
They reveal the character of Christian worship.
Paul does not celebrate confusion for its own sake.
He does not treat disorder as proof of divine power.
He does not encourage believers to abandon understanding.
In fact, he repeatedly emphasizes intelligibility, interpretation, and the strengthening of the congregation.

In 1 Corinthians 14:27–28, Paul instructs that public speaking in tongues should be limited, orderly, and interpreted. Without an interpreter, the speaker is to remain silent in the church and speak to himself and to God.
That alone should challenge much of what is casually defended as biblical worship.
If someone insists that every uncontrolled public manifestation must be accepted without examination, Paul does not agree.
If someone claims that interpretation is unnecessary because the experience feels powerful, Paul does not agree.
And if someone suggests that spiritual authenticity is measured by the volume of the room, Paul does not agree.
The Holy Spirit is not honored by ignoring the instructions He inspired.
There is also a necessary distinction between the clearly identifiable human languages spoken at Pentecost and the more difficult discussion of tongues in 1 Corinthians 12–14.

Christians disagree about whether all biblical tongues were recognizable human languages or whether Paul's discussion may also encompass speech not understood by ordinary hearers without interpretation.

First Corinthians 13:1 mentions "tongues of men and of angels," but the verse is part of Paul's rhetorical argument about the supremacy of love; it should not be treated by itself as conclusive proof of a separate angelic prayer language.
We must not claim certainty where the text requires careful interpretation.
And now we need to talk about prophecy.
Because for some readers, this is where the deepest wounds are hiding.
Perhaps someone once looked into your eyes and said, "God told me you are going to marry this person."
You believed them.
You rearranged your hopes around their words.
You ignored warning signs.
And when everything collapsed, you wondered whether you had somehow failed God.
Perhaps someone prophesied healing over a sick loved one.
They spoke with confidence.
They promised a miracle.
But the healing did not come.
And when you were already drowning in grief, someone suggested your family simply hadn't possessed enough faith.
Or maybe a leader used the words "God told me" to control your decisions, silence your questions, or keep you from leaving a harmful environment.
If that happened, the problem was not that you asked too many questions.
The problem was that a human claim to divine authority was used in a way that demanded more trust than Scripture permits.
The Bible never tells Christians to accept every spiritual claim unquestioningly.
First Thessalonians 5:20–21 says:
"Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good."
And 1 John 4:1 warns:
"Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world."
The Greek word δοκιμάζετε (dokimazete), used in 1 John 4:1 for testing, carries the idea of examining or evaluating.
Not blindly accepting.
Not automatically rejecting.
Testing.
This is not unbelief.
This is obedience.
In 1 Corinthians 14:29, Paul says:
"Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge."
The Greek verb translated "judge" is related to διακρίνω (diakrinō), which can mean to distinguish, evaluate, or discern.
Even in a congregation where prophecy was operating, prophetic speech was not to escape evaluation.
Think about the implications.
A person saying "God told me" does not remove the responsibility to examine what was said.
A dramatic delivery does not establish truth.
Tears do not establish truth.
A large following does not establish truth.
And a message that contradicts the Gospel does not become holy because someone spoke it while trembling.
Scripture gives severe warnings against false prophecy.
Deuteronomy 18:20–22 warns against speaking presumptuously in God's name, and Deuteronomy 13:1–3 teaches that even an impressive sign must not lead God's people away from Him.
The New Testament likewise warns against false prophets and deceptive signs.
Christians disagree about the precise relationship between Old Testament prophecy, foundational apostolic revelation, and any noncanonical prophetic activity claimed today.
But there is no biblical permission to excuse manipulation, false doctrine, or careless predictions merely because someone claims a spiritual gift.
And we should be especially cautious about those who repeatedly make predictions, refuse accountability, and then blame the wounded when their words fail.
God's name is too holy to be used as a shield against correction.
If you have been harmed by spiritual manipulation, you do not have to abandon Jesus to reject what was done in His name.
The Shepherd is not the same as the person who misrepresented Him.
You can grieve what happened.
You can seek wise pastoral counsel.
You can examine Scripture again.
And you can rediscover that Christ does not need fear, coercion, or manufactured certainty to lead His people.
But there is another danger on the opposite side.
We can become so afraid of deception that we begin to treat every testimony of God's extraordinary work with contempt.
We can become proud of our skepticism.
We can mistake emotional distance for theological maturity.
We can speak accurately about doctrine while refusing to pray with expectancy.
And we can forget that the living God is not confined by our inability to explain everything He may choose to do.
God is sovereign.
He hears prayer.
He heals according to His wisdom.
He acts in providence.
He can do what human strength cannot accomplish.
Believing that certain revelatory gifts have ceased does not require believing that God has become inactive.
And believing that the gifts may continue does not require believing every modern claim.
Both sides should be able to confess that Jesus Christ is alive, that the Holy Spirit indwells believers, and that God remains free to act according to His will.
What we must never do is reduce the Holy Spirit to a religious technique.
He is not a force we activate by repeating a phrase.
He is not an atmosphere we manufacture through music.
He is not a reward for emotional intensity.
He is the divine Person who gives life, glorifies Christ, convicts of sin, strengthens believers, and works according to the will of God.
And this brings us to the most devastating part of Paul's teaching.
Because immediately after discussing spiritual gifts, Paul writes words that should make every gifted person tremble.
"Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal."
—1 Corinthians 13:1, KJV
Then he goes further.
"And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing."
—1 Corinthians 13:2, KJV
Nothing.
Not merely less effective.
Not simply immature.
Nothing.
The Greek word for love here is ἀγάπη (agapē).
In this chapter, Paul describes love through patience, kindness, humility, truthfulness, endurance, and the refusal to seek selfish advantage.
Imagine possessing extraordinary religious abilities and yet failing at the very love those gifts were supposed to serve.
Imagine having a voice that moves thousands but a heart that refuses to forgive one person.
Imagine being celebrated for your prophetic insight while your own children are starving for your kindness.
Imagine winning every theological argument and losing your compassion for the people Jesus died to redeem.
That is the tragedy Paul is confronting.
And it is a tragedy that can happen in charismatic churches and non-charismatic churches alike.
One congregation may idolize manifestations.
Another may idolize intellectual superiority.
One may confuse excitement with holiness.
Another may confuse emotional restraint with holiness.
One may excuse false claims because they sound supernatural.
Another may dismiss sincere believers because their experiences do not fit its expectations.
But Jesus calls all of us to something deeper.
He calls us to Himself.
Remember the words of Jesus in Matthew 7:22–23.
Many will say to Him, "Lord, Lord," and appeal to prophecy, exorcisms, and mighty works performed in His name.
Yet Jesus warns that some will hear the dreadful words:
"I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity."
This passage is not teaching that spiritual gifts are inherently false.
It is teaching something far more frightening.
Religious activity—even activity that appears extraordinary—is not a substitute for truly belonging to Christ.
The question is not merely whether people are impressed by what you do.
The question is whether you know the Lord.
And whether your life is being brought under His authority.
You may have an unforgettable testimony.
You may have witnessed something you cannot explain.
You may be able to defend every detail of your denomination's position.
But have you repented of your sins?
Are you trusting in the crucified and risen Jesus?
Are you learning to love the people around you?
Are you submitting to the truth of Scripture?
Are you becoming more humble, more truthful, more merciful?
Because Galatians 5:22–23 describes the fruit of the Spirit as love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faithfulness, meekness, and self-control.
And although spiritual gifts and spiritual fruit are not the same thing, the fruit of the Spirit matters profoundly when evaluating spiritual life.
A person may claim to possess a remarkable gift.
But no claim of giftedness excuses a life of unrepentant cruelty.
No prophecy makes pride holy.
No tongue makes dishonesty acceptable.
No miracle gives anyone permission to exploit God's people.
And no theological position makes lovelessness a virtue.
Perhaps you came into this article expecting a simple verdict.
Yes, the gifts continue.
Or no, the gifts have ceased.
But Scripture is pressing us toward a larger and more searching question.
What are we doing with the Jesus whom the Holy Spirit came to glorify?
Here is where I stand in approaching this question from the biblical text.

I do not believe Scripture gives us sufficient grounds to declare that God is incapable of granting tongues or prophecy today, or that every modern claim must be false simply because the apostolic era has ended.

The language of 1 Corinthians 13, particularly its movement toward knowing fully and seeing face to face, provides a serious reason to question the claim that the completion of the biblical canon is the clearly stated moment when all such gifts ceased.

At the same time, Scripture gives us no permission to assume that every modern manifestation is genuine, that every believer must possess the same gift, or that contemporary prophecy carries authority equal to the inspired words of the apostles and prophets preserved in Scripture.
The safest biblical posture is neither reckless acceptance nor automatic dismissal.
It is humble openness to God's sovereign work, firm submission to the Scriptures, careful testing of claims, and unwavering devotion to Jesus Christ.
This is a continuationist-leaning conclusion, not a declaration that every faithful Christian must agree with it.
Faithful cessationist Christians offer serious biblical arguments, especially concerning the foundational role of the apostles and prophets and the final authority of Scripture.
They deserve a fair hearing.
But whichever position we hold, we must not make agreement on the continuation of every spiritual gift the test of whether someone belongs to Christ.
The Gospel is too precious to be displaced by that debate.
And now I want to speak to the person who has quietly felt spiritually inadequate.
You have been comparing your prayer life to someone else's.
You have been wondering why your hands don't tremble the way theirs do.
Why you haven't received a vision.
Why you don't speak in tongues.
Why God seems to answer other people's prayers with extraordinary stories while your own life feels painfully ordinary.
You get up early.
You work.
You struggle with bills.
You try to forgive.
You battle temptation.
You pray over your children.
You open your Bible when you're exhausted.
You keep trusting Jesus even when nothing spectacular happens.
And somewhere along the way, you started believing that your quiet faithfulness wasn't enough.
Please hear what Scripture actually says.
The Spirit distributes gifts according to His will.
The body has many members.
The eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of thee" (1 Corinthians 12:21).
And the parts that seem weaker are indispensable to the life of the body (1 Corinthians 12:22).
Your place in Christ's body is not determined by how impressive you appear.
The believer quietly caring for a sick parent may be demonstrating extraordinary Christlike love.
The Christian resisting a secret temptation may be fighting a battle no congregation will ever applaud.
The exhausted mother praying over her sleeping children may be exercising a faith that heaven sees even when nobody else does.
The wounded believer who chooses to forgive may be displaying the transforming grace of God.
And the person who continues trusting Christ through unanswered questions is not necessarily less spiritual than the person with a dramatic testimony.
Do not despise the ordinary means by which God shapes His people.
Prayer.
Scripture.
Repentance.
Worship.
Fellowship.
Service.
Faithfulness.
Love.
These are not consolation prizes for Christians who lack spectacular experiences.
They are central to the life of discipleship.
And to the person who believes God has genuinely worked through an extraordinary gift in your life, hear this with equal tenderness.
You do not need to exaggerate what happened to make God look powerful.
You do not need to defend every questionable manifestation to prove you believe in the Holy Spirit.
You do not need to turn your experience into a universal requirement for everyone else.
If God has entrusted you with a gift, use it with humility.
Submit it to Scripture.
Welcome wise examination.
Serve the Church.
Refuse personal glory.
And remember that the Giver is infinitely greater than the gift.
The Holy Spirit does not need your exaggeration.
Jesus does not need your performance.
And God's glory is not strengthened by claims that are untrue.
Sometimes the holiest words a believer can say are, "I believe God can do this, but I need to test whether this particular claim is true."
Sometimes the most courageous words are, "I was wrong."
And sometimes the most Christlike response is to embrace a brother or sister who disagrees with you while remaining faithful to your biblical convictions.
That is not compromise.
That is maturity.
And perhaps the deepest scandal in this entire conversation is that Christians can spend decades debating the gifts of the Spirit while neglecting the Gospel that brought them into God's family.
We argue over tongues while refusing to control our own tongues.
We debate prophecy while ignoring the clear commands of Scripture.
We pursue healing while withholding forgiveness.
We speak about revival while resisting repentance.
We seek signs of divine power while overlooking the cross, where the power and wisdom of God were displayed in a crucified Messiah.
But the cross is where our boasting dies.
The cross tells the charismatic believer, "Your experiences cannot save you."
The cross tells the cessationist believer, "Your theological precision cannot save you."
The cross tells the wounded believer, "Your suffering has not placed you beyond My grace."
And the cross tells every sinner, "You cannot redeem yourself."
Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He welcomed the weary.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He healed the afflicted.
He proclaimed the Kingdom.
He was betrayed, mocked, condemned, and crucified.
And on that cross, He bore the penalty of sin as the righteous Savior of the unrighteous.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
This is not a spiritual manifestation competing for our attention.
This is the Gospel itself.
The foundation of Christian hope.
The message Paul declared to be of first importance in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
And it is through this Jesus that sinners receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
The greatest need of the human heart is not to have a more impressive testimony than the person beside us.
It is to be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
What good would it do to speak in every language on earth if your heart remained far from Him?
What good would it do to correctly predict tomorrow if you refused to surrender today?
What good would it do to win a thousand debates about spiritual gifts while rejecting the grace that alone can save you?
And what a beautiful thing it is when someone who once chased religious approval finally rests in Christ.
When someone manipulated by false spiritual authority discovers the gentleness of the true Shepherd.
When someone proud of spiritual experiences bows in repentance.
When someone proud of theological knowledge learns to love.
When someone who believed they were spiritually worthless discovers that they are welcomed by grace through faith in Jesus.
That is transformation.
That is redemption.
That is the story of scandal meeting grace.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because deception didn't matter.
Not because truth was optional.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save, forgive, restore, and transform those who turn to Him.
And maybe this is the moment you need to stop asking whether you have experienced enough to impress other Christians.
Maybe you need to ask whether you have surrendered your life to the Savior.
Maybe you need to repent of spiritual pride.
Maybe you need to repent of judging believers whose experiences differ from yours.
Maybe you need to walk away from a ministry that uses God's name to control people.
Maybe you need to stop using past disappointment as a reason to avoid prayer.
Maybe you need to open your Bible again, not to win an argument, but to hear the truth of the God who loves His people.
And maybe, for the first time in a long time, you need to pray something simple.

"Lord Jesus, I don't want to chase power and miss Your presence. I don't want to defend doctrine without love. I don't want to mistake emotion for truth, or fear for discernment. Forgive my pride. Heal what deception has wounded. Teach me to honor Your Word. Fill my life with the fruit of Your Spirit. Give me whatever gifts You desire, and help me use everything You give for Your glory. Above all, make me more like You. Amen."
If this article has exposed something you have been afraid to admit, you do not have to pretend.
Maybe you have felt rejected because you don't speak in tongues.
Maybe you have been wounded by a false prophecy.
Maybe you have been too quick to judge.
Maybe you have witnessed something you still cannot explain.
Or maybe your heart simply longs to know Jesus more deeply.

And if you are comfortable, tell us where you are in this journey. Do you believe the gifts continue, have they ceased, or are you still studying the Scriptures? Have you experienced something that changed your understanding?
You do not have to reveal painful details publicly. Your honesty can be as simple as "I'm still learning" or "Pray for me."
Let the conversation be marked by Scripture, humility, and love rather than accusations.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, don't ignore that thought.
Perhaps it is the friend who has been told they aren't spiritual enough.
Perhaps it is a family member who was hurt by a religious leader.
Perhaps it is someone who has become cynical about everything supernatural.
Or perhaps it is a believer who loves the gifts of the Spirit but needs a reminder that love, holiness, and biblical accountability must never be abandoned.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
Not because an algorithm can produce revival.
But because a thoughtful, Scripture-rooted conversation may reach someone who would never walk into a church or ask a pastor these questions.
Return to 1 Corinthians 12–14.
Read Acts 2.
Study Joel 2.
Examine 1 Thessalonians 5 and 1 John 4.
Don't simply remember what this article said.
Test it against Scripture.
That is how mature disciples grow.
Invite your family.
Your friends.
The Christian who is struggling.
The believer who has become lukewarm.
The seeker who is asking difficult questions.
Even the person who does not yet believe in Jesus.
There is room to hear the Gospel, wrestle honestly with Scripture, and discover why Christ remains our only Savior and ultimate hope.
And we want to do more than create posts that people read once and forget.
We want to help people become serious students of Scripture and faithful followers of Jesus.
These resources are part of our commitment to making biblical encouragement and discipleship accessible.
But sustaining and expanding this work requires real support.
Writing, research, resource development, distribution, and ongoing ministry efforts all involve time, labor, and expenses.
And this is where you can become more than a reader.
Scripture teaches us in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That means your decision must be free.
No pressure.
No guilt.
You can glorify God through generosity, but you cannot purchase His approval.
Jesus already paid the price of our redemption.
What we are inviting you into is not a transaction for spiritual favor.
It is an opportunity for partnership.
These products are simply practical resources and reminders that can encourage faith-filled living. They are not substitutes for the Bible, the local church, or genuine discipleship.
Pray for the ministry.
Save these Scriptures for deeper study.
Because the mission is not to build an audience that admires Gospel Warrior.
The mission is to point people to Jesus.
And when all the debates have ended, when every microphone has gone silent, when every earthly ministry has completed its work, one truth will remain.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Our spiritual gifts will never be greater than Him.
Our experiences will never outrank His Word.
Our traditions will never replace His Gospel.
And our greatest hope will never rest in what we can do for God, but in what Jesus Christ has accomplished for sinners.
One day, faith will become sight.
We will no longer see dimly.
The questions that have troubled us will find their proper place before the glory of God.
And every redeemed voice will have one infinitely worthy object of worship.
Not the gift.
Not the experience.
Not the preacher.
Not the denomination.
The Lamb who was slain.
The Savior who rose.
The King who reigns forever.
So yes, study the gifts.
Ask the hard questions.
Test the claims.
Honor the Scriptures.
Pray with expectancy.
Exercise discernment.
Love the Church.
But never become so consumed with asking whether tongues and prophecy are still active that you neglect the far greater question of whether your own heart is surrendered to the living Christ.
Because the deepest evidence of grace is not that you have become impressive in the eyes of people.
It is that a sinner who once lived far from God is being transformed by the mercy of Jesus.
And when every extraordinary voice has fallen silent, the nail-scarred hands of Jesus will still be enough to tell you how deeply you are loved.
